name: Bombard an area
summary: The unit picks a spot, often far beyond its own gun's reach, and after a delay something heavy lands there: shells, a missile, a glob of acid, bombs from called-in jets or a beam from orbit. The delay is the heart of it: a visible warning (a marker, a flare, incoming aircraft, a laser dot, falling bombs) gives the enemy time to scatter, so the caster must predict where they will be, or hit what cannot move (deployed units, buildings, a revive, a capture). Some versions make the caster keep designating the target until impact and call the strike off if that stops; in some the delivery can be shot down on the way. Most hurt whatever stands in the area, friend or foe.
counterplay: Watch for the warning and leave the marked area before impact.
Kill or interrupt the designator: a held strike is called off when its caster dies or the beam breaks (Boris, the StarCraft II Ghost's nuke).
Shoot the delivery down: anti-air downs called-in jets, and point defence can stop incoming missiles.
Disarm a planted beacon before its countdown ends.
Keep moving and spread out; strikes punish stationary and clumped targets.
Deny the caster sight of its target with smoke, cloak or a shroud field, and hunt it while it is busy aiming.

other_examples.note: The Ravager lobs a glob at a ground spot at long range, and it comes down a couple of seconds later, hurting ground and air units alike. Players use it to crack defences and force fields and to make enemy armies move out of the way or be hit.

sources.title: Corrosive Bile (Ravager page), Liquipedia StarCraft II Wiki

other_examples.note: The Ghost marks a spot and must keep targeting it through a long countdown before the warhead lands. The enemy sees only a small red dot while the caster's side sees the whole blast area. Killing the Ghost or pushing it out of range during the countdown cancels the strike, and the blast hurts both sides.

sources.title: Tactical Nuke, Liquipedia StarCraft II Wiki

other_examples.note: The mortar crew can order a quick salvo of a few shells onto a ground point at range, with a minimum distance, on a cooldown it shares with its smoke barrage. The mortar's scatter makes it unreliable against moving infantry, but a barrage shifts enemies holding fixed positions, and a shell that lands on a building harms the whole garrison.

sources.title: PM-41 82mm Mortar Squad, Company of Heroes Wiki

shooter_analogues.unit: GS-2 ion cannon beacon (and the Nod nuclear strike beacon)
shooter_analogues.note: A soldier sets the beacon down; after a long countdown an ion cannon strike hits that spot. The defending team can stop it by getting to the beacon and disarming it, engineers being trained for that, so the planting team has to guard it. In multiplayer, a beacon on the enemy base's pedestal wins the match.

Her ultimate: she throws a flare, and rows of missiles land in front of it, each bursting several seconds after it lands, so a wave of blasts creeps forward. The blasts hurt and slow enemies, only slow squadmates, and an enemy Wattson's defensive pylon can destroy both the flare and the missiles in flight.

His ultimate: he picks a spot on a tactical map that reaches only so far around him; a short charge-up that every player can see and hear warns of it, then a laser fills the area, hurting anyone inside and blocking sight until it shrinks away.

player_translation.summary: A key that marks a spot at long range; after a warning both teams can see, a strike lands there. The player trades instant damage for reach and power, and wins by predicting where enemies will be or by hitting what cannot move away.
as_user: Press, place the target circle (on screen, or on a zoomed-out map for the longest strikes), confirm; the strike lands after a set delay.
Lead your targets: aim at the choke they must cross, the point they must hold, a deployed vehicle or a teammate being revived, never at a player who is already running.
Designator versions keep you exposed: you hold the beam on the target until impact and cannot fire meanwhile.
Earned versions are a reward: an objective (sabotaging an airfield, a streak) gives you one strike to spend when it matters most.
as_target: A warning (circle, flare, laser dot or jets coming in from the edge) appears at the spot with a rising sound; leave it or get behind hard cover.
If someone is lasing it, hunt the designator: killing them or breaking the beam cancels the strike.
Shoot down the incoming aircraft or missiles if your unit can reach them.
Deployed and slow units cannot get clear in time, so pack up or move as soon as a marker appears near you.
teammates: Setup and finisher: a teammate's stun, slow or pull keeps enemies in the circle until impact.
Spotters matter: a scout or a reveal finds targets beyond the caster's own sight.
The enemy team coordinates its answer: anti-air or point defence to intercept, a fast unit to hunt the designator, an engineer to disarm a planted beacon.
Versions that hurt allies make teammates clear the circle too.
controls: Q enters targeting: a circle follows the cursor up to the maximum range (a map view for off-screen strikes); left mouse confirms, right mouse cancels.
Designator variant: hold Q to keep the beam on the target until impact; letting go, a stun or death calls the strike off.
Earned and one-shot variants show their charge on the HUD and use the same key.
feedback: A team-coloured marker on the ground at the target that both teams see, with a shrinking ring or countdown and a rising sound.
The delivery shows from above: jets crossing from the map edge, a streak of shells, a beam forming from above.
A large but brief blast with camera shake near it, then a scorch mark.
A minimap ping at the target for both teams, and a distinct alarm for players standing inside the circle.
Designator variant: a visible laser line from caster to target, so the enemy can trace it back.
changes_from_rts: RTS strikes often come from buildings or side-wide powers (the parabombs a spy earns, superweapon beacons); here the strike lives on one player-controlled unit with a cooldown or a charge.

Huge one-shot strikes (Boris levelling a building, a nuke) must be scaled down: strong enough to clear a point or wreck a deployed vehicle, but always escapable by an alert player who sees the warning.
Boris's airstrike can only target buildings; here a strike should hit anything in the circle, with structures and stationary units as its natural prey.
The warning must be readable by the target from above; StarCraft II's small red dot for the enemy is too subtle for a top-down shooter.
Off-screen range needs a map view or a spotter, because a top-down camera cannot aim at what it cannot see.
A one-time earned strike (the Red Alert 1 spy's parabombs) becomes a charge earned from an objective, not a permanent key.

team_play.notes: Teammates hold enemies in the circle and spot targets beyond sight; a designator needs bodyguards while it lases; the enemy team needs anti-air, point defence or a hunter to stop the strike.

notes: A delayed area hit is simple; the work is in the targeting interface (circle, range limit, map view) and in a warning both teams see in time.
Called-in aircraft or missiles that can be shot down need their own flight paths, health and interception rules.
Designator variants need a held beam with line-of-sight checks and abort rules (caster killed, stunned, out of range).
The strike's timing and area must be server-authoritative so the warning shown is honest.
Long-range, heavy strikes can camp spawns or snipe objectives from safety; cap the range at about two screens and give a long cooldown.
Against stationary targets (deployed units, revives) a strike can be unavoidable; deployed units need time to pack up, and the warning must be long enough.
Several players' strikes stacked on one point wipe it; consider limiting charges per team or reducing damage from overlapping strikes.
The target must see the warning early enough to react, or the strike feels unfair.
Several overlapping markers in a big fight need team colours and a countdown on each.
Players inside a circle must see its marker even when the caster is far off screen.

variants.name: Called strike
variants.summary: Pick a spot; after a short visible warning the strike lands there.
variants.seen_in: StarCraft II Ravager Corrosive Bile; Valorant Brimstone's Orbital Strike

variants.name: Salvo
variants.summary: A few shells in quick succession scatter around the spot: good against what stays put, unreliable against what moves.
variants.seen_in: Company of Heroes 2 mortar teams' barrage

variants.name: Held designator
variants.summary: Keep a beam on the target until the strike lands; it is called off if you let go, are stunned or die, and you cannot fire meanwhile.
variants.seen_in: Red Alert 2 Boris (MiG airstrike); StarCraft II Ghost Tactical Nuke

adds_weaknesses.why: The strike lands only after a warning, so alert, mobile enemies step out of it; it pays off mostly on slow or stationary targets.
It must stand exposed and hold the beam until impact, unable to fight, and the strike is lost if it is interrupted.

variants.name: Interceptable flight
variants.summary: The strike arrives by aircraft or missiles that can be shot down on the way, so anti-air and point defence are a real answer.
variants.seen_in: Red Alert 2 Boris's MiGs; Red Alert 1 parabombs dropped by bombers; Apex Legends Bangalore's missiles against an interception pylon

countered_by.why: Fast units are out of the circle long before impact and can close on the caster.
Flankers reach the caster while it is busy aiming or lasing a target far away.
Anti-air shoots down the called-in aircraft or missiles before they reach the target.
Point defence picks the incoming missiles out of the air.

variants.name: Creeping barrage
variants.summary: Rows of blasts land in a line that advances away from the marker, sweeping a strip of ground instead of one spot.
variants.seen_in: Apex Legends Bangalore's Rolling Thunder; the Red Alert 1 parabomb run drops its bombs in a line

variants.name: Planted beacon
variants.summary: Plant a beacon at the spot; after a long countdown a devastating strike lands unless an enemy reaches the beacon and disarms it, so your team must guard it.
variants.seen_in: C&C Renegade ion cannon and nuclear strike beacons

countered_by.why: Fast units are out of the circle long before impact and can close on the caster.
Flankers catch the planter while it is busy setting the beacon down at the target.
Engineers reach the planted beacon and disarm it before the countdown ends.

variants.name: Earned charge
variants.summary: No cooldown: an objective (sabotaging a building, a streak of kills) earns one strike, kept until used.
variants.seen_in: Red Alert 1 Spy (one parabomb strike for each enemy Airfield it gets into)

variants.name: Doomsday strike
variants.summary: A huge, slow strike: a very long warning, a very large area, harm to friend and foe, and one use per life.
variants.seen_in: StarCraft II Tactical Nuke; Renegade superweapon beacons

adds_strengths.why: Hits a spot far beyond its own gun's reach, hard enough to clear a point or wreck a deployed vehicle.

adds_weaknesses.why: The strike lands only after a warning, so alert, mobile enemies step out of it; it pays off mostly on slow or stationary targets.

counters.why: Buildings, turrets and deployables cannot dodge the strike.
Deployed units cannot pack up and leave before impact.
Slow units cannot clear the marked area in time.

countered_by.why: Fast units are out of the circle long before impact and can close on the caster.
Flankers reach the caster while it is busy aiming or lasing a target far away.

open_questions: How far may a strike reach: within the caster's screen, or anywhere a teammate can see? (Recommended: about two screens; a map view only for off-screen variants.)
Should the target see the whole blast area or only a small dot, as StarCraft II shows the enemy? (Recommended: the whole area, for fairness from above.)
Should strikes hurt teammates? (Recommended: reduced damage to allies.)
Should a held designator, which takes the player out of the fight, be allowed below T3?

shooter_fit.reason: Called strikes are common in shooters (Renegade beacons, Apex and Valorant ultimates) and read well from above as ground markers; they need a fair warning and a long cooldown to avoid unavoidable damage and objective camping.
